title: Chapter 42 – Elder Mu
html:
[Blood Shadow Sect – Elder Mu]

Elder Mu prunes his weeping lilies before dawn, because it is the only hour of the day when no one is allowed to speak to him.

The garden is a small one, a cold stone courtyard at the back of a house on the Frostfang ridge, forty miles northeast of any place a Sect inspector would think to look. There are twelve beds, each a ring of black soil bordered with white pebbles, and in each bed grows a single lily the color of old milk. They droop. That is their nature. Each stem bends in a long slow arc toward the ground, and each blossom hangs like a bell with its mouth turned down. He has coaxed them for thirty years. He feeds them a thimbleful of a certain red tea, once a week, on the night of the new moon, and in the spring they answer him with a smell so faint and sweet that visitors mistake it for their own memory of someone they loved.

He kneels in the cold with a pair of small bronze shears. He is eighty-two years old and looks forty-five, a lean, clean-shaven man in a plain gray scholar's robe with ink on his cuff and the gentle, slightly stooped manner of a teacher who has never once raised his voice at a pupil. His hair is black. His hands are very clean. When he clips a withered petal he does it as one might close a child's eyes.

"Elder," says a voice behind him, softly.

He does not turn. "It is not yet light, Lei."

"I know. I am sorry." A pause. "A reply has come."

The shears stop.

There are, in all the Blood Shadow Sect, perhaps six men whom Mu would permit to interrupt this hour, and his scribe is not one of them. But Lei is a scrupulous creature, thin and middle-aged, a Qi Refining fifth-stage with a limp and a long sad face, who has kept the Elder's records for eighteen years and has never been known to be wrong about what mattered. If he has come, it matters.

Mu rises, and wipes the shears on his sleeve, and turns.

* * *

The letter is on good paper, which is the first surprise.

It is smooth, pale, fine-grained, with a faint sheen like skin. It has been folded in three, and sealed with a plain wax thumb-mark, no crest. Lei has opened it with a knife and laid it on the stone bench in the lamplight, as flat as a leaf. The brush-strokes on it are steady and black and beautifully made, in the unhurried hand of a man who has never in his life needed to hurry.

To whom it may concern, at the stone cairn where the Salt Road meets the river.

I regret to inform you that the guest elder of this house is unwell and cannot attend. His health has not allowed him to travel. His book is not for sale. He has asked me to say that he is grateful for the courtesy of the invitation, and that he is not in a position to accept it.

The Hill of Green Pine sends its regards, and wishes you a peaceful spring.

Lin Wenyuan, Patriarch.

Mu reads it twice. Then he reads it a third time, slowly, with his lips slightly parted, and a look comes over his long, quiet face that Lei has seen perhaps four times in eighteen years.

He is smiling.

"A peaceful spring," he says.

"Elder?"

"I have been writing letters to the stupid and the frightened for sixty years, Lei. They answer in two ways. They grovel, or they threaten. I do not remember the last time anyone thanked me." He lays his fingertip on the final line. "He has made me a courteous refusal in a perfect hand, and told me that his guest is too ill to travel, and signed it with his own name. He is not afraid of me. He does not know what I am. Or he knows, and has decided that it is not enough to matter." The smile fades. "I find I would like to meet this man."

"The cart-driver found it under the cairn at dawn. Weighted with a stone." Lei pauses. "There was also a second thing."

"Yes?"

"A pebble, Elder. Round. Quite ordinary. It had been set on top of the note." The scribe's long face creases. "I did not understand it. I thought perhaps a joke."

Mu is silent for a moment.

"Show me."

Lei takes it from his sleeve. It lies in his palm, a small pale oval no bigger than a quail's egg, smooth as a worn coin, with a faint pearly sheen. Mu does not touch it. He bends over it, and looks, and his dark eyes narrow.

It is not a pebble. It is a scale.

* * *

The room where Mu receives his people is a long low chamber with a fire at one end and a window at the other. A table runs down the middle. It is not a council table. Mu has always disliked the sort of sect that hangs its hall with banners and gives its elders carved chairs. It is a plain pine kitchen table, scrubbed white, with six stools and a pot of millet wine kept warm on a brazier.

He sits at the head with his hands folded and listens.

They are four, and they have come in the night. He does not need to look at them to know them. He has chosen them himself over three weeks, with the care of a man selecting tools for a delicate job.

Bone Tally sits nearest the fire, a vast, soft, pale man in a hooded cloak of tattered black leather, with a drum on his knees. The drum is made of the skin of a drowned man, stretched over a ring of knee-bone, and it is very beautiful, with a pattern of tiny red spirals pricked into the surface. He strokes it with one thumb. He is a Qi Refining ninth-stage, a Drip of the first rank, and he has not spoken a word in public for eleven years. It is said that the sound of his voice is the one noise he cannot bear.

Across from him, side by side, sit the Drip Sisters. They are twins, thin, sallow, black-haired women of thirty, in rust-colored cloaks and identical expressions of mild boredom. Mei Lian is the elder by a minute. Mei Ru is the better shot. Each has a length of black chain wound three times around her right forearm, and each chain ends in a barbed hook, and the hooks are connected, at the heart of each, by a hair-fine thread of blood that runs from one sister's wrist to the other's. They are both Qi Refining eighth-stage. Together, in a close fight, they can pass for something better.

At the far end of the table, on a stool by himself, a short brown man with a broken nose and a placid face sits with a hound at his feet. The hound is gaunt and gray and silent, with eyes like wet coals. It is a beast of the first rank, medium tier. Its master, whom everyone calls Shan, has been a tracker for the sect since before Mu was an Elder. He smells of horse and old blood and smoke. He has the great and rare virtue of never saying anything he does not know.

"You have read the letter," Mu says.

Nobody answers. It is not a question.

"The Lin Patriarch is polite. His house is not stupid. They have laid pins in the ground. They have a ring, I am told, of Yellow-grade iron, around a stone hut in the quarry. They have an old artisan who was once the finest refiner in the Eastern Sea, and who is, at present, drinking himself to death in an old granary." Mu lifts the cup. "They have also, it seems, killed four of ours."

Mei Ru stirs. "Four, Elder?"

"The two hired. A rogue called the Fog, and another. And two of the Drips I sent to the northern forest in the autumn, who did not return." He sips. "Lei has been through the lockets."

Lei, standing at his shoulder, clears his throat. "A Drip's blood-locket records the moment of death, Elders, sisters. A last impression. A scrap of sense. It is not reliable. It is a feeling, not a picture. But in the case of the first scout, the thin one, I was able to recover something."

"What?" says Mei Lian.

"A needle." Lei's voice is flat. "A thin one. It went in at the right collarbone. Through a gap in the Qi shell, the gap at the join of the shoulder, where a trained man covers with his arm. The scout was not covering. He was looking at something else." A small pause. "He felt the needle go in. He thought it was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen."

Nobody says anything.

"And he felt," Lei goes on, more slowly, "that he was being seen through. Not looked at. Seen through. As if the shell had been transparent."

"A seamwalker," says Shan. It is the first thing he has said. His voice is a dry rasp. "A seamwalker can do that. They see a barrier the way a rat sees a wall. They know where the wood is thin."

"Yes. That is what I thought." Mu sets down the cup. "A young one. A hatchling. It had been wounded; the scouts had been sent to take it. And someone on that slope has taken it instead. Someone who knows what it is, and has used it, within a week of finding it, to kill two Drips." His fingers drum softly on the pine. "Who?"

"The old artisan," says Mei Lian.

"No. The artisan has a bent rod and one arm. A drunk old man does not use a seamwalker's sense to drive a needle into a collarbone." Mu shakes his head. "The Patriarch is a talisman drawer. His brother is a captain of mortals. The woman, Su Qinghe, is a Qi Refining fourth-stage, quick with water and a knife. It is not her style. It is not anyone's style." He pauses. "There was a smaller impression, in the locket. At the very end. The scout's eyes, as he fell. He saw the tree."

"What tree?"

"A dead oak. And in the oak, high up, lying along a branch, a shape." Mu's voice is very gentle. "He thought it was a child's."

For a moment nobody breathes. Then Mei Ru laughs, a short, scornful, nervous sound.

"A child."

"Yes."

"A boy. Ten, eleven."

"I did say a shape." Mu's mild eyes rest on her. "The locket is not reliable. I would not put my life on it. But I have been doing this for sixty years, and I find that I have developed a respect for small details." He folds his hands again. "There is a boy on that hill. A pseudo-root, with five dim crystals, a quiet one. The steward of Red Ridge has mentioned him three times in the last year, in connection with various small impossibilities. A man named Gu Yan, my pupil, died in a cave a year ago and spoke of him with his last breath. I have been told that the boy counts." He lifts one shoulder. "I have been told nothing else. That is, as a rule, the sign of someone worth remembering."

* * *

Before the bone-lots, Mu does one more thing, and he does it alone.

He takes the scale to the cellar. The cage stands there on a wooden trestle, a squat box of black iron strapped with strips of bone, no longer than a man's forearm. Every bar is etched with the same tight, repeating knot. A Coral Gate sigil, a cousin of the one that guards the Founder's Pool, drawn small. It is meant to hold anything that passes through walls.

He sets the scale on the floor of the cage, and shuts the door, and steps back.

The scale does nothing. It lies pale and still on the black iron, as a scale should. Mu waits for a count of fifty. Then, because he is a careful man, he crouches and watches the knots on the bars for any sign of strain.

The nearest knot flickers. Once. As a lamp flickers when a door opens somewhere in the house.

It reaches for the seam from here, he thinks. Through forty miles of rock and a month of silence, a dead scale reaches for the gap in the weave. He feels something cold and pleasant move in his chest, the feeling of a man who has found the last stair in the dark. So the hatchling is real. And it is near enough to the hill that its own shed scale still answers it.

He opens the cage and takes the scale back. It is slightly warm.

"Do not hurt it," he says again, to the empty cellar. It is a strange thing to say aloud. He cannot say to whom.

Upstairs, the hound Shan keeps is whining at the door. It has smelled the scale through two floors of stone, and it has not stopped shivering since.

It is Lei who brings the bone-lots, after the others have eaten.

He has an old woman with him, bent and brown and toothless, in a coat of patched wool, who walks with two sticks and has to be helped to the stool. She is called Auntie Sump. She is a geomancer. She has served the Blood Shadow for sixty years, and for fifty of those she has read the veins of the earth the way other women read a husband's temper. She carries in her lap a bowl of fine gray sand, and in the sand, a handful of knucklebones.

"Auntie," Mu says, with real warmth. "It is good to see you out of the cold."

"I am not out of it. I am going back to it." Her voice is a creak. She scatters the bones across the sand with a flick of her wrist. "You asked about the hill. You asked me a month ago, and I told you. Green Pine's vein is dying. A little every year. A fraction of a hair."

"Yes."

"It is not dying now."

Mu goes very still.

"It is dropping," says the old woman. She bends over the bowl. Her toothless mouth works. "Three parts in a hundred, it has been, since the midsummer. I have listened to it every new moon. Steady as a sick man's heart. Three parts. And then four nights ago." She prods a bone with one crooked finger. "One."

"One?"

"One part in a hundred. For three nights running. It came back, a little, on the fourth." She leans back. "A vein does not do that, Elder. A vein fades. It does not stutter. It does not hold its breath. What it does is what a man's pulse does when a hand is laid over his mouth. Something is taking it. Something under the hill, deeper than the vein, is drawing it in."

"The door," Lei breathes.

"I do not know what the door is, boy, and I do not wish to." Auntie Sump pokes the bones into a heap. "I only know that when a vein goes quiet, a house built on it goes quiet too. Walls fail. Formations sag. A ring that was laid in the autumn with ten thousand strokes of an old man's hammer, and fed from the vein, will be thin as paper this week." She raises her small, bright, ancient eyes. "It will not last. It might be three nights. It might be seven."

"And after that?"

"After that the vein comes back, or it does not. I cannot tell you which."

Mu sits very still. In the fire a log shifts and falls in a soft shower of sparks.

"You have done well, Auntie," he says at last. "I thank you. Lei will see you are fed and put in the warm room."

She grunts, and gets up on her sticks, and goes out with her bowl. The door closes behind her.

"Four nights," Mu says.

"Elder?"

"The window may be three nights or seven. I would like to use it before it closes." He turns to the table. "Tally. Sisters. Shan. A cart of spirit-iron ingots leaves Green Pine Hill every ninth day, to a refiner at Willow Ford. It goes by the Salt Road for eleven miles, through a place called the Narrows, where the track is a shelf between a cliff and a stream. It is guarded by a captain of the clan and four to eight men. It was, until this morning, the only regular movement out of that hill that is not a Sect courier." He lifts a finger. "It will be there in two days."

"We take the cart," says Mei Lian.

"You take the cart. You take it quickly, with the drum, and you do not stop to talk. You kill the captain, because he will not give up the road. You kill whoever else stands. You leave one man alive, to run home with the news." His voice has not altered at all. It is the voice of a man ordering a meal. "I want the hill to know that I can reach it. I want them to learn what it costs to say no to me in a beautiful hand."

"And the smith?" says Shan.

"Will not be there. He is in the granary, with his wine. I want him alive, and I want him afraid. He is more useful afraid." Mu's gaze moves along the table. "And the seamwalker."

Nobody speaks.

"If you see it, take it. Alive. There is a cage, a thing of black iron and bone, in the cart outside. Do not hurt it. It is the size of a loaf. It will bite, and it will try to go through anything that is closed. Use the cage. Do not let it touch a wall." His voice drops. "It is not a pet. It is the second half of a key, and I will not have it spoiled."

"And the boy?" says Mei Ru, with a kind of delicate unease.

Mu smiles.

"If there is a boy," he says, "I want him very much."

"Alive?"

"I want to see him."

"Elder." It is Bone Tally. It is the first time in the whole of the night that he has spoken, and the voice that comes out of the vast pale hood is a high, thin, cracked whisper, almost a child's. "I will take the drum."

"I would be disappointed if you did not."

"A boy cannot stand a drum." A slow, wet smile spreads across the soft face. "Not a small one. His channels are too narrow. I will stun the road at fifteen paces. I will stun the cliff." He strokes the skin with one thumb. "Nothing living that is under the seventh stage will still be standing when I have finished. And nothing that is hiding in a tree."

"Good." Mu rises. "Then we are agreed. I will be at the border, at the old inn at Three Willows, a half-day's ride from the Narrows. I will not come in. I will wait to hear what you find." He pauses. "I do not wish to be there. I wish to be told."

The four of them stand. They do not bow. It is not the Blood Shadow's custom. Each of them draws a small knife, and pricks a thumb, and lets a drop of blood fall into the cup of millet wine on the table, and Mu stirs it with his finger and drinks it down.

"Go," he says.

* * *

He is alone in the long room, at the table, with the cold fire and the empty cups, when Lei returns.

The scribe stands in the doorway for a time without saying anything. He holds a small clay jar in both hands. It is warm. The steam from it rises in a soft, fragrant curl, sweet and thin and sad, the smell of a dream half remembered.

"Your tea, Elder."

"Thank you." Mu takes it. He cups it between his palms, and does not drink. "You have something else."

"I would not presume."

"Lei. I have known you eighteen years."

The thin man's face works. "I wonder whether it was wise," he says slowly, "to tell Bone Tally of the child. He is not a man who is careful. He will use the drum on whatever he sees. If the boy is a small, quiet, ordinary pseudo-root, it does not matter. If he is not—"

"If he is not, then he will have to be very quick." Mu looks at the steam. "I want to know what he is, Lei. I have spent three weeks looking at the shape of this thing from the outside, and I find that the more I look, the less I understand. A dead rogue, a dead pupil, a dead pair of scouts, a patient old man with a gift for slag, and a pangolin on a doorstep." His long fingers tighten on the jar. "If I put a man in front of it with a very large drum, I will see what moves."

"And if it kills him?"

"Then I will have learned the thing I wished to." Mu's voice is gentle. "That is what the drummer is for. I do not like to waste a good drummer. But I do not like to be afraid of a ten-year-old either."

Lei says nothing. He has long ago given up trying to tell, from the Elder's face, whether a given sentence is a joke.

Mu rises. He crosses to the window, with the jar in his hand, and looks out at the garden, where the twelve lilies hang pale and bowed in the first gray light. Beyond the wall the ridge falls away into blue mist, and beyond that, forty miles off, a hill that he has never seen sleeps under its pines.

The Founder's Pool is sealed with a Coral Gate lock, he thinks. And the lock has no keyhole. It has a seam. A hair-fine gap in the weave that only a seamwalker can taste. And a hand that knows the Canon to make the key.

He thinks of his master, three hundred and twelve years old and dying in a cold cell of the Rill stage, with his blood going to ash and his last hope sealed behind a door that no living man has opened. He thinks of Elder Jue, his rival, who has been whispering in the Rill's ear that the old man's time is up, and that the Pool Gate should be opened by someone younger and more obedient. He thinks of the long, soft, ambitious years, and the many small cruelties he has done in the name of patience.

The smith. The seamwalker. And the door.

Three pieces. I have found two on one hillside. It would be a very great pity if it turned out that I had misjudged the third.

He drinks the tea. It tastes of lilies and iron, and something sweeter underneath, like the memory of a face.

"Lei," he says.

"Elder?"

"Send word to the border. I will not wait at Three Willows. I will go on, as far as the river." He sets down the jar. "A man should see the ground he is about to take. I am told the Narrows are very beautiful in spring."

The scribe bows. He goes out, softly, closing the door behind him.

Mu stands alone at the window for a long time. The sun comes up. The lilies lift their pale bells to the light, and in the garden the first small birds begin, one by one, to sing.

It is a perfectly ordinary morning. It smells of blood.
